projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Edward F. Brandtner was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II Veteran Edward F. Brandtner. Mr. Brandtner served in the U.S. Army, with the 9th Infantry Division, 39th Regiment, Company I. He served in the European Theater and his highest rank was Corporal. Ed was a POW. I'm Tom Swope and this interview was recorded at Mr. Brandtner's home at Maple Heights, Ohio, on May 12, 2004. Ed was 84 at the time of this recording. Tom Swope: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: I was living in Maple Heights.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: In Maple Heights?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: I was born here and raised here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And I was born on McCracken Road in 1920, and when my parents moved there in 1918, March 14, 1918. My sister, next oldest sister, she was born May 13, 1918. She was born -- my mother was pregnant when they moved in and my mother always said that when... we had a well, it was just like a farm. We had a well and an outhouse, and she was... she use to take the water out of Mill Creek. I don't know if you know where it's... if you come down 480 you come over the bridge.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum, yeah.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: That's Mill Creek and it runs from all the way from Beechwood all the way down to the canal. And right on -- oh, it would be Broadway and Miles, there's a waterfall. And when we were kids we always walked from our house on McCracken, we walked down... well first we walked up to the creek up to Beechwood and when we ended up, there was a little spring, then we turned around. A couple of days later we walked the other way and all the way down to the canal -- the canal river.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So in 1941, were you in college or were you out of school?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: No. I was, I was...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Working?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yes. I was working at that time. I was working at Shawnberger (ph) on Harbor and Broadway.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And I registered for the draft in July of '41.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And, well at that time it was -- wasn't bad. Well, there was fighting in China with the Japanese and then Hitler took over the European countries.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7, 1941?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Oh yes. I was... when I... I worked in a theater on Broadway and Maple Heights. It's right across from Maple Town; right now it's a Music Manner. Anyway, I was working... I started 12:30 and they open up the box office at one o'clock and then they start the theater... the show started at 1:30. Well, I got... I went home to eat. And anyway, when I got in the car I turned on the radio and they said, "Pearl Harbor was bombed." And when I come back I told the people that didn't know... know about it and I told them about it and they wouldn't believe it. Then later on after... later on it came over... they had it over the loud speakers that Pearl Harbor was bombed, but a lot of people already knew about it and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reaction when you heard that news?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: I was shocked. Because we were well... we weren't well prepared for that war. And I was very... I had a couple of buddies that were in Pearl Harbor at that time, one was in the Navy and the other one was in the Army, that I grew up with. They joined the Army in 1938. So they had three years in when the war broke out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did many of your friends decide to go out and sign up immediately?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: I tried to enlist, but I had bad teeth, and they they didn't want to take me. And that was in December. And January 23rd I got a notice for a physical. I took my physical and I was 1A, and a month later I was in the Army.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And I was inducted in Camp Perry, Ohio. From there I was there for... from Sun... Monday 'till Friday and then we left. We were sent down to Fort McClellan, Alabama. I took my basic training in infantry. And in May we left Fort McClellan and I was shipped out to Campo, California. I joined a tank destroyer battalion.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And -- I... well, I had infantry training. I knew about the compass and that and I was teaching... teaching some of the people about using a compass, and I went from a Private right up to a T5. Well, I was a gunner on a tank destroyer. It was a half-track 75 millimeter utility piece. And then in July --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I was going to ask you, when you first went into the Army, was it a tough adjustment to be in there with guys from all over the country?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Well, I knew some of the fellows I was drafted with, there was a couple from Maple -- one from Maple Heights and one from Garfield Heights that I got to be... you know very close. And anyway... but after we left Camp... Fort McClellan, well, they split us up. There was a couple of... when I was drafted we had quite a few boys... fellas that I knew from Maple Heights; most of them... the majority of them were sent to the Air Force.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any stories from your training that you recall before you went overseas?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Well, we took a lot of training. Well, like I said, rifle we fired. At that time they didn't have bazookas or... they had rifle grenades but they didn't have no bazookas. And the rifle that I had was an Enfield rifle. That was a British rifle, and boy that had a kick to it. And I had a pretty good... while I was a kid my dad showed me how to shoot, and I had a good... I was a pretty good marksmen and I was getting bulleyes and the Sergeant tapped me on the shoulder, he said, "you want to be a"... what do they call them again? Background: Sniper.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Sniper.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sniper, Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And he said -- I said "no." He said, "well you better lay off." So I started getting couple Maggie’s drawers. And then I had... I was taught how to fire quite a few weapons. Well, we fought... I mean, we had a Gerand, not a Gerand. They were like a machine gun.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: BAR maybe.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: BAR yeah. That was a good weapon.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Then from there when we went to California. I was assigned with a Tommy gun.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Then we went through more training, grenades and stuff like that. And two different outfits that I was in, tank destroyers. I pretty... got hurt one day. On a Saturday morning we went to grenade... tossing grenades, and one guy... they brought the cooks in to throw the grenades. Well, he threw it and it bounced back into the trench, and I grabbed it and just threw it over the... over the... I was standing near him, and I grabbed it and threw it right over the top, and it went off, and there was shrapnel inside the... inside the trench, and then the cook got hell. And we -- from Camp... Camp Coachella we went to the desert maneuvers and we were there from July 'till November, and then we had... we were with the two... armored division. They were training them toward an invasion of Africa. And then we... I saw General Patton.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And we were supposed to have been knocked out. And he come in with a tank and he said, "what... what's the matter with you guys?" And we said, "why, we're knocked out." And he said, "oh no you aren't. That... that field artillery piece on a moun"... like on a plateau is not split trail. They didn't take it out off the truck and they were supposed to knock us out. So he said, "Get that gun and fire and knock them out." And so I did. And then from there we all saluted him and then he took off. And then later on we heard that when we first time went on a desert in July, there was a town by the name of India -- Indio and they... the people in that town wanted to make the town off limits. And Patton went up there and he said, "no." He said, "you keep it open for the troops." And anyway he said, "if you don't want your wives or daughters messed up, keep them locked up." He was a... oh, he had a bad mouth.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So he probably didn't quite say it in that language, right?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: No, no, he swore. And then when the maneuvers ended we stayed there until November. And the days were warm but the nights were cold. And if you had your water in a canteen, the next morning it was freezing, crack your canteen open. Well, then from there we went to Camp Hood, Texas and at that time it was -- I got my first furlough in January of '43. And then, when we came back from our furlough, and then we went on... well see, I was a gunner on a tank destroyer. And then fine... finally I... I... when I came back I took... I had a tank destroyer patch put on my shoulder and our Company Commander asked me why I put it on. I said, "well, I belong to a tank destroyer. And he... then he -- then he said, "okay, the Battalion Commander okayed it. You can have a patch." And we -- then we stayed in camp... camp... we were... we moved to Camp Atterbury, and from there I had a good time. I used to come home every weekend. And then we went on a Tennessee maneuvers in July of '43, and we were there until September of '43, and then I come home for another furlough, and then we went back to Camp Atterbury. And we were there from... there 'till January 29th of '44, then we were shipped overseas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your designation for your outfit?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: What do you mean?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, you were a tank destroyer battalion?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Oh yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the number?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: I was in two, 705.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And 773rd.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And attached to a particular division?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Well, we weren't attached to the 705 Division, but later on we were attached to the 99th Infantry Division.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right, Okay.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And then in -- after we... when we were... our outfit, the tank destroyer battalion, was sent down to the southern part of England to get the troops ready. They worked in a mess hall. And I stayed with the vehicles to keep the guns clean. I had to take good care of four tank destroyers in our... in our platoon. And anyway, after then...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything about that crossing to England? Any stories from that?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Oh yeah, in 29th of January, we went overseas on the Aquitania, that was a British ship. And there was... I guess over 4,000 troops on that... and nurses and officers. And we were with a group, I forget what the group was, number. But we were fed only one... twice a day; 10 o'clock in the morning and 10 o'clock at night. And after breakfast they let us go on top of the deck, to you know... and it was... it was cold, well, it was January and then in February. And we landed in England... no, in Scotland, and then we went down into England. And we were in a little town by the name of Stone on the Wall, our battalion. That was a little village. And we stayed in a Lord's... well, I don't know if he was a Lord or what, his home. I guess the government took over his estate. And then from there that's when we... our troops went down to southern part of England. And I went to a little town in... outside between Birmingham and Coventry. And then I... I had my... every day I got my pass and I went to Coventry. And then we were there...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was Coventry still in pretty bad shape from the --

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Oh yeah, oh yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It was?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: There was a church that was bombed.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And they made -- you could go in there and you had to pay so much to go in there and you go in the second floor and you go look over the town in Coventry. That was a nice town. And then -- and then we... after the invasion we went back to southern part of England and I joined the outfit, and I stayed with the outfit about a month. But then I... our First Sergeant, I lent him some money in the states, and I kept asking for it. And he told me he don't owe me no money, "I don't owe you any money." And anyway, I kept after him because I didn’t... I was broken down to a Private, and I was just getting so much money, and they took out my laundry and everything, and I was just out of money... running out of money. And then finally I got angry because he put me on KP one day and guard the next day. And I did that for three weeks straight. So I got... I got a little angry, and I went to see the Company Commander and I ask for... to see him, and he said... and then I asked him... told him about that, and he said, "Sergeant, can I have the duty roster." And then he asked, "why is he doing it." And he said, "I was a troublemaker." I wasn't no troublemaker, but because I was asking for my money.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And then I asked for a transfer. And I said, "I can't take that anymore." And ended up at the 9th in a replacement pool. Then in... that was in August. And then in... I stayed in a pool for a month, and then we were shipped into Le Mans, France. And then I... for awhile, and then I was taken into a combat area and I joined the 9th Infantry Division.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you got to France probably what, September of '44?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You got to France probably in September of '44?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And then I -- then I got transferred into infantry... 9th Infantry.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Into the 9th, Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yeah, and the 29th of -- I joined an outfit, the 29th of September.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And that's when we started going through that Hürtgen Forest.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first -- was that your first combat then?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Hürtgen Forest?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yeah, that was my first combat.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember your first day in combat then?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yeah, oh yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What are your memories of that day?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: It was rough. That was a forest, and it was... it was terrible fighting in that. I got a... there's a book "The Bloody Forest." I sent for it. And then I got some stuff that... about the forest and where we were captured. I got captured October 10, 1944.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: In the Hürtgen Forest?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Hürtgen Forest.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: I don't know if you ever heard of the Hürtgen Forest.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yes, I have. Yes, I talked to a couple of guys that were there.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. So what else can you describe about the fighting in that forest?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Well, I'll tell you something, it was -- we didn't make very much headway every day. And then it was rough, because we were fighting in a forest, and they had a lot of Germans sent artillery all the time. They shoot artillery at you and they hit the top of the tree. Well, it was mostly pine trees. And then you get a tree burst plus shrapnel. And twice I left, I went on night... at night I went on guard, and I come back and my blanket was perforated with shrapnel. If I would have been in there, I would have been killed. But I always went closer to the tree, because you know why? That's the least... least you can get hurt. Because if it's further away, then you get a lot of that shrapnel, it would be like a colon (ph).

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Did you lose any buddies in the forest there?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Oh yeah. We lost... that's why when we... we got captured at six o'clock in the morning, October the 10th... well, the night before we took this little village, one part of the town. It was an abandoned sawmill. And when we took it at dusk... well, the Germans were on one side and we were on the other side. And they put us in... on guard. We had to pull guard duty, and then it was six o'clock... well it was about four o'clock. They started with mortar and then some artillery, but we all hid under the... in back, you know the sawmill with saws and planers and that. It was just like a shelter. And six o'clock I just... we just got off of guard duty and was just going to lay down, and all of a sudden the Germans said, "come out, come out." Well, we went out and I... when I surrendered I was in such a shock, I surrendered with my rifle in my, in my... holding it up. And my buddy kept... a friend of mine kept hitting me, "drop it, drop it," and anyway, I finally dropped it. And then they searched us, they made us undress, and it was raining that -- and cold, and they let us put our clothes... clothes back on, but they took some of the money away from us... and us... and I had some English money and then German... not German, American. Then I had an American silver dollar that my dad gave me, and then they let me keep it. And then after one we were in another camp outside of -- I can't think, it was a marshland in Germany. Anyway they... they... the camp, and then Americans were bombing this marshland... Bonn, and they were bombing it. And then the one B-17 was circling over, and all of a sudden an 88 went right up into the bombay. They just opened up the bombay, and the plane exploded. And the only person left... that lived out of that plane was the tail gunner. And that evening they brought him into camp. They... he was all blooded up because the civilians caught him and they beat him up. And then the next morning he was gone. And well, see they kept their Air Force away from ground troops. And then we... then we ended up in XII-A, a prison camp that was our station. That's when they registered us as prisoners of war. And we were there from about October 12th or 13th, and then they -- November the 20th... no, 16th, we left hammers... the town, Limburg. And we... they shipped us all the way into Poland. And we were in a town by the name of Hammerstein that was II-B because the POWs in our chapter were there. And then we were there from the 20th of November, and we went... after then we went to... well, we spent Christmas. We were getting Red Cross parcels. Then in January they decided they were going to pull us out of camp and put us in another camp. Then the Germans decided to keep us there, let us stay there. And then the morning of the 29th, they moved us out... out of the camp. And there was a big blizzard. That day it was snowing and cold, and they put us on a road. And that night I froze my... well, that night I froze my feet. And then I took my... like a dummy, when we stopped that night to put on my... I tried to put my shoes on... that was... was second time. And I left... left... oh, that's right. I left my shoes on. But the first time I froze my feet going on a train to II-B. I took my shoes off because we stayed all day, and it was raining and my feet got wet, and when they put us in a boxcar, they locked it and there was gaps in the floor about an inch and a half, about two inches, and all that cold air was coming in through the box cars. And then when I got to the II-B they... they... they had a medic there and he... he's... he was in the other... he was a Staff... Staff Sergeant. And anyway they... they... he works with the medics, and later on I'll tell you more about him. Then they put us... they deloused -- deloused us and... give us a shower and deloused us and then they put us in these barracks. Well, anyway we -- we were... we had Americans and British and Canadian soldiers and in that camp they had Serbs and then they had some French... French soldiers, and they worked in town. The French worked in a town. But they had... they could bring bread in and they were selling it to us. Well, we were paying two packs of cigarettes for a loaf of bread. And we got the Red Cross parcels. We had... I'll give you... I'll show... maybe I'll make you a copy of the Red Cross parcel.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Of what was in the parcel?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you -- you had to share a parcel with how many guys?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Well, at first we -- when we were in II... XII-A there were ten of us sharing a parcel, there wasn't much that you could get. But then when we were in II-B, well... we... two... two men shared a parcel, my buddy and I.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhmm.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And then like when -- on the 29th of January, every so often they brought us on the road, they give us a parcel, to... you know. If it wouldn't have been for the Red Cross parcel, we would have starved. But my buddy and I were... were little thieves, too. We used to steal stuff from the Germans. And we... we bribed a German guard, and we'd give him a couple... couple of cigarettes and he'd turn his back, we used to run... see, the German farmers would bury food... vegetables in the ground.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Umhumm.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Well, when you see a big mound, you knew there were some vegetables in there. And even if the ground... the ground was frozen, we... we still broke up with our heels and that got the... got the food. My buddy used to do the kicking and I used to do the, with my hands... you know, getting... breaking up. And we had rutabagas and cabbage, onions, carrots, and anything vegetable, potatoes. And then we... that night we... we'd eat and we'd cook. And my buddy and I, we always carried a big pot with us that we traded a German civilian for a... for a couple of cigarettes. We got a nice pot. We had spoons. And well, we got the spoons right away. And a fork we got in a prison camp, we had to get it... buy it from the Germans. And then... but then... well, we walking from January 29th through May 1st.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were on the road that long?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: We were on the road that long. And then in the winter time we were in the barns. And when it started getting warmer... then as soon as they... well, when we were... we were... when we left the camp, there were 1900 of us, and then they broke us up in a group of 90. Well, once... once they broke us up in a group, they started going different directions. So we... we slept in barns and that. But once it started getting warm, they let us... we had to sleep outside. But we got two blankets. So my buddy had two blankets and we put two blankets on the ground and then two blankets covering us. I still talk to that fella. And anyway, when we got liberated May 1, 1945, and in a Bürgermeister farm, and when we got liberated, the Russians come with motorcycles and they had a Tommy gun on their shoulder and they told us stay there because -- don't leave because we get... you know, they'll notify... they won't bomb us or come in. Then later on in the afternoon the group came in. But they'd... I hated them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The Russians?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: I hated the Russians because they treated us bad.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did they? What did they do?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Well, they -- well, we had... I... I... we had... they took watches, some of the guys' watches and rings. And they... they... well, we didn't have no money. They couldn't take the money, but they took the watches and rings. They were thieves just like... well, the Germans... I think the Germans were better than they were. And then that... that afternoon, well, that morning the... we had a Colonel, a Captain and two enlisted... four enlisted men that were guarding us. Anyway, they changed clothes and they left. Well, three... two days later we found them, they were killed by the Germans... by the Russians. They shot them in the... in the field. And I picked up a Mauser rifle, I kept it all the time 'till I got on the ship. And anyway, I'm going too far.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, where were you when you were liberated?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: We were east of the Elbe River. We were about I'd say 60 kilometers east of the Rhine... Elbe River.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, so that's still in Germany, right?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yeah, that was East Germany.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum, yeah.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And then when we left that house -- farm, we had two hay wagons and two tractors so we confiscated and then we took the two vehicles. Well, there were 45 guys on one... one... one hay wagon. And anyway we...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So were you allowed to just go back to American lines then?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No? You just left?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: No, no, no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Got scared?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Because after we were liberated by the Russians, we had to make our own way to the Elbe River. Once we got to the Elbe River, we got there 4:30 in the afternoon, and the Russians wouldn't let us cross the river. And they kept arguing that we're Germans. And we kept saying, "no Americans, Americans. "No Germans, Nein Germans, Deutsch, Deutsch." And then finally the British saw us. That was one good thing that the British saw us. And anyway they... they started negotiating with the Russians. And finally there were Generals, Russian General and a British General, they... they said, "okay cross." But I'll tell you something, there's a lot of POWs that are back in Russia, they took back and... and that's what they wanted to do to us, too. We were so close to liberated... being liberated, and it's funny that they didn't do that when... when we first got... we got first liberated, and then...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you dressed as POWs though? Wearing your POW...

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: No, we wore American uniforms.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And that time you still had your American uniforms on?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, we had American uniforms.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So they just were trying to pretend that --

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- maybe you had put on American --

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- uniforms to get out?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: But I wanted to tell you when we first ended up in II-B, we had to turn in our uniforms.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And they took our -- everything; GI shirts, pants, and even the... I had a field jacket, they took that away from me. And then they, well, at that time we didn't have no overcoats with them... with us. And anyway then we were issued by the Red Cross the... the overcoats. We had... we got... later on we got winter underwear and everything. But after we got into West Germany, we were with the First British Army. And we got there May 7th. On May 8th they had signed the armistice. The, you know... the Germans surrendered. Then Montgomery come into the First Army headquarters there and he inspected us. He inspected... well, they lined us up with the British and Americans, and there was quite a few Americans in there that were liberated. And then Montgomery came by. Then when he come to us, as he passed us he said, "British American." How did he say it again? "Bloody American" and then he said something and one guy swore at him. American guy, he was two guys away from me. And he said... he swore at him, and he turned around and said, "Who said that?" And we started laughing. Oh, he got mad. And he walked off and didn't even... didn't even finish inspecting us, because we looked like... hey, when you come out... we were dirty, our uniforms were, you know, torn, and anyway...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So was he criticizing your appearance?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yeah, well, he said -- well, he hated the Americans.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh yeah.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And anyway, we got hell from the British Field Marshal, another general. He said... he said, you know, British Field Marshal. One guy said, "yeah he... he swore at him, too. He's an asshole." And... and well, see he's... he's the one that caused our getting captured in Hürtgen Forest.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, how's that?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: He's the one -- he's the one that planned it, him and Bradley, to send the 9th Division into that forest.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum, right. The whole idea of going through the forest, which was not a smart idea, right?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yeah, because --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He was in the planning of that?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yeah. Anyway they... they after... then the British that... British General he said, "you insulted a Field Marshal," and what can you do? And well, he didn't have no business saying "Bloody Yanks," you know. He should have said nice things about us because we were supporting the British. And then from there we stayed there for a while, and then we went to Lübeck, Germany. And then they were flying the Americans... B17 were flying the... some of the POWs into Camp Lucky Strike, France. And then I went on a Lancaster British bomber. They flew us to England. And then we went to England, and then we stayed in this Air Force Base for two days, and they gave us all new uniforms and stuff. We took showers and that. Because we... our stomachs were big because we were... malnutrition and that. And then from... we went... they sent us to an Army hospital. We were in there four days, and then they shipped us... we got Class A passes in London, and we were there from... 'till June 6, 1945. And then from... we got on a LST and come home to the United States on a LST. That was a rough ride.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when did you get to see your family then?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: When I hit -- we landed in Newport News. And then there was an Army Base there and they sent us there. And I called home. I reversed the charges to my folks and I told them I'm in the United States. They were real happy. And from there they sent us to Camp Atterbury. We stayed there for two days. On June 28th, 1945, I came home on a furlough and I was home on a furlough from June 28th, I left June... I mean September, I think it was 20th. I went back to... they sent me all the way down to Fort Sam Houston, Texas. All that distance. I stayed there. And I... they finally... they give me... they had to pull my upper plate... I mean teeth. And then they... after they pulled my teeth, I had to wait to make a plate. And then they sent my... accidently they sent my service records to California. And then I had to wait a couple of days for... to get them back. So I got discharged November the 24th of '45. I came home and I... I well, I... I told people about being a POW, but they... they... at that time it didn't register. But I had a buddy of mine, he got killed on Okinawa. We were drafted together. And he... they sent him to Camp... a camp in Fort... Fort Lee in New Jersey. From there he went to San Francisco and they shipped all those to Honolulu. He was... they was... he was there all that time. He took his basic and all that in... in... in Hawaii and in Honolulu, outside of Honolulu, and then he was with a field artillery. And then in May on invasion of Okinawa he got killed. 25 years old.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How long was it before your family found out that you were actually a prisoner of war?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: My first letter.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: From XII-

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: I sent them a letter and they got it through the international. That was in, I think, in January. I think I still... I... I... I had it. I don't know. But then... then a... then an Adjutant General sent them a telegram that I was a prisoner of war. But they knew -- already knew it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Because they had gotten word through the Red Cross?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Red Cross, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right, that the -- now was the Germans reading a list on the radio? Is that how that happened?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: No, no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The Red Cross was just getting a list?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Well, they -- see I was registered with the... with the... as a POW.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you went to that, what was it, XII-A you said. Is that when you were registered?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: XII-A, yeah. XII-A they registered me there. They didn't notify the American Red Cross... I mean the International Red Cross I was a prisoner of war. No. Yeah, but see I was...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But the Red Cross knew about it before the Army knew about it?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Oh yeah. They sent my mother... I... well, I... I wrote at home. That was the first one. They got it, then the Red Cross notified them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Then -- then the Army sent them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you able to get any mail from them after that?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: No. No, I didn't get any mail from... from August on.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: From August of '44. Were you able to keep up at all in the... in the prison camp on the war news? Anybody smuggle --

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: There was all rumors always.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: They started rumors that the war was going to end in November of '44. Then in December. And then when they had Battle of the Bulge, there was... they brought some POWs from the 106th in there. But then... then they sent them on a farm. See, I was lucky. Because they... they kept me in a camp. My buddy, anybody that had a German name.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: They kept in a camp. Or... or -- well, I had a friend of mine, well, he looked Italian. Then I finally found out he was Jewish. Well, they... they sent... they sent... they... they kept him in a camp. He was in the same barracks as I was. He was from Cleveland. There were quite a few guys from Cleveland in my barracks. There were Rangers and then there were some from 82nd Airborne, 101st Airborne, because they got captured in... in Holland.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: That was a -- that was a terrible thing. That was when Montgomery messed up.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: You know the British, I don't know if you knew that the British had a habit of stopping at 4 o'clock and having tea. Well, that's what happened. They stopped to have tea, and then... actually Montgomery knew that the tanks were there. Because they had photographs of the tanks in that... in that... you know -- and he still went up there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So overall the Americans didn't think much of Montgomery?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: I didn't care for him -- a lot of guys. And Patton never... never liked him.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. What else can you tell me about life in the prison camp before you were on the road?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Well, it was boring. And... but I kept... kept saying I'm coming back, I'm coming back. I read a lot of books. And... and we had a... we had a wind-up record player, we used to play that, and then... and then we had... camp had a band. They used to have shows. We used to go every Sunday. We go to... for service. Well, no, it was in the evening about 7-8 o'clock we went to the chapel. They had a chapel there. We had a guy that was a minister, he did the services. Boy, he was good. And I asked this guy that... I told you, he was a... worked with the medics. I met him in 19... what was it... '80... '80, '89 and in Niagara Falls. He sat at our table and I kept looking at him. He looked so much familiar. And anyway, I asked him what outfit... where... what camp was he in. He said "II-B." And then he said -- I asked him... he said... told me... he said I had -- I told him I was in II-B, too. And he said, "when did you come in?" I told him in November. He said, "you come in with the group that they took... and then they took your uniforms away?" And I said "yeah." And then he said, "you know what those uniforms were for? They used them for the Battle of Bulge."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Infiltrate.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Because our uniforms were pretty good, you know. They were battle... they were trench worn but they... they weren't torn or nothing. And we were issued British uniforms, and that... that wool was itchy. See because our... our uniforms were gabardine, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Were you in the service?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No, I wasn't. My father was.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: I know. What outfit was your dad in?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He was in the 103rd.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: In Germany too, huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They were captured in the Alsace-Lorraine area, near the Vosges Mountains. And he was captured on December 1st or 2nd, late in the night. I think it was December 2nd about the time they were captured, yeah. I was going to ask you, oh that Jewish soldier, did he throw away his dog tags so they couldn't identify him?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They just never checked?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Just like Sal, Sal (ph) had his --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right, I know, that's why I asked.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: They had the star -- that had the dog tags.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, a star or an H or something.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yeah, a star -- star.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And I -- I've heard stories some guys just lying about that when they got their... being told to lie about that when they got their dog tags. But he... he just got... hmm. He was lucky.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: I tell you, I belonged to the DAB.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And our past commander, he disliked the POWs. END OF SIDE ONE BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE. You could never say anything about POWs. He said... one day... one... we have a guy in our chapter, his name is Phil Monroe. And every time we have a meeting he always brings up about the POW. And I keep telling him, "Phil, keep your mouth shut. This is a different... different, outfit, you know, chapter."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And anyway, he mentioned about -- about the POWs this Andy Kowalski (ph,) he was very... I don't know, he hated... he disliked the POWs. He told me, "you should have fought 'till you got... 'till you got killed." He said, "I hate... I dislike the POWs. They gave up without fighting." I told him we were fighting. What are we going to do when you're... when you're surrounded? Are you going to try to get out of it?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, my dad -- 98 guys were surrounded.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I mean, that's a big group of guys. Obviously they were surrounded by a division. There's not a whole lot...

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yeah, we -- we were surrounded by the Wild Figera Company (ph) that was over... over 100 people.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right, sure. 150, whatever. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: I was in -- the company I was in "I," anyway, our company commander and then the lieutenant were down in the basement in the sawmill, and they... they come up at 10 o'clock. Everything was quiet. And then the Germans were surprised that they nailed them then. I always... always wondered what happened to them guys, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. So they did get captured though?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When they finally came up.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Well, figured 10 hours later -- I mean, four hours later.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. You mentioned the nerve things, did you have any other troubles adjusting to civilian life after the war?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Oh, I had -- I had a lot of problems. I had... I had horrible dreams, and my wife... my wife could tell that. I... I jumped out of the... a lot of times I'd be sleeping, I jumped out of the bed. I'm running in my sleep. And then one night I... I... it was lucky... I was fighting, and all of a sudden I had my fist doubled up. If I wouldn't have woke up that second, I would have hit her right in the jaw. I would have broke her jaw. I had horrible dreams. And I... I'll tell you something, when I... I had started having this problem after I got out of the Army. And anyway, I drank heavy, and I... I still did, but I got to cut it out because I'm taking a lot of medication now. But I'll tell you, that's the time they should have had something prepared for the prisoners of war. Because that -- that... that brought me... I had nerve problem. I... I... I had nightmares. And when I took... when... 1983 I went for PSD. And I went... I... see they disallowed me... the Army... I mean the VA, was very stingy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: So I had to go before the board in -- in... in V

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: .. each town, and I had to go between one doctor... two doctors. One was a psychiatrist and the other one was a doctor. And they kept asking me questions. But I had a guy that did the... he was from the DAB. He had my... you know, told them stuff, and then the doctor would say, "how about you, sir, what?" You know, I told them I had such... I'll tell you, when I was at the end, I had two guys, miserable guys, that worked with me. I worked for the City of Maple Heights. And these two guys would light up a cigarette, both of them light it up, inhale, turn, face me and blow the smoke in my face. They did that... they did that to me all the time. I told the foreman about it. He say, "Hey, don't be a baby." And I told that to this doctor, the psychiatrist. You know what he told me? If that would happen now you have a good... good... you could sue the both of them. Because I got emphysema from them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right, exactly. And they did that to you all the time?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: They did that to me 'till finally I -- I told the foreman I said I don't... oh, I got a... I... I took a... I... I became a driver. Then I... I... but then one died. He retired, a year later he... he died. And this other one, he lived about three years and he died. One died of cancer... lung cancer and the other one died... and I knew that one. I grew up with him. He lived in Maple Heights. And I knew him real good. But he was a miserable... most miserable man I ever saw. I tried to help... do stuff for him, and the more I did it, the more he'd make fun out of me. And one day he started saying, he said, "if your nose gets any bigger and your ears get bigger you'll be able to fly." I came right back at him and I said, "okay, shake and bake," because he shook. From that day on I quiet him... I quiet him down.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think about your experiences during the war, does any other particularly vivid memories come to mind?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Little bit. Oh yeah. Well, I traveled a lot of camps, and then the best one I liked was in Camp Coachella, California and Camp Atterbury, because I used to come home every weekend.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: I used to get a pass. We get a pass at 12 o'clock Saturday and we were supposed to be back in camp by midnight of Monday morning. We never get... got back to camp 'till 6 o'clock, 5 o'clock in the morning. It all depend what time that train got in to Indianapolis. We leave Cleveland, at 9 o'clock and figure that took... it took at least six hours to drive from Indianapolis to Cleveland because they stop... they made a lot of stops.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So as long as you got there before roll call, it was okay?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Well, yeah. Well, I was lucky. Because we had... the First Sergeant was with us. And most of the... they were from Cleveland, so they...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: So they would have had to -- they would have had to... well, they couldn't court-martial us, but they could make a company punishment, you know. But we... I was a Corporal at that time. So then... most of them were noncoms, you know, and some of the Privates. But we... there was quite a few from Maple... I mean Cleveland. I still touch... get in touch with a guy from the 773rd. He's in... he lives on the east... west side, and he put me on with the... with the 773rd Tank Destroyers. You know, I still get letters from them, I mean from the division.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The time you were in England, before you went to France, did you get along okay with the English, British people?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: I got along British. Yeah, they were... lot of people, they liked the Americans. You know why? They spent money. I... what... what we were making... we were making as equivalent a Captain or Major was, you know, in the English Army. They weren't making... they weren't making nothing compared to what we were getting.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. So the people liked you, but not necessarily the soldiers, the British soldiers?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Well, they were jealous of us. Yeah. But I met some Germans... British soldiers that were POWs. And -- and... oh, I can tell you one thing that I forgot to say. One night while we were on a road they put us in a barracks... I mean a barn. In the upstairs were chickens. Somehow one of the guys got in it, and when we left... the next morning when we left, there were no chickens left. Well, my... we... my buddy and I got two chickens. And we stripped them by, you know, without even boiling them, and just pulled the feathers out. And then... then we cut them in pieces and buried the intestines and everything in... underneath the hay... straw. Anyway, the next morning they woke us up and they marched us... marched us out of town. They told us to drop our stuff. So we had, my buddy and I, had a little suitcase that we got when we got registered as POWs. So anyway, we had cups and stuff with us. And anyway, so they started searching us. And my buddy and I... we had an overcoat. So we... what we did, we cut the chickens in half, in quarters and in half, and we put them... wrapped them up in our underwear, clean underwear. Anyway they... Germans didn't think of searching... searching the coat. And there were about six of us that had... did the same thing. Well, that night we were cooking... making... we got water and we got vegetables, we were cooking the chicken in the thing. This German guard kept walking, good, good, good. And so after my buddy and I, we got through eating, we made hogs out of ourselves, and then... then we saved some for the next morning... on... when we were walking, you know. But the... this German guard, after you give him some chicken and some broth in the thing, he was our friend. Every time we point... you know. But he got killed, like I told you. He got... he was...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He was one of those that got killed.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: He was about 68 years-old. They could hardly walk, but they were guarding us. And they could hardly walk. Sometimes we carried their rifle for them. But they didn't... they didn't have no ammunition, you know. They were afraid, you know, if we get together we could take their ammunition... I mean, their rifles away and kill them, but...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was he also a guard in the camp then, that you were in?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yeah, he was a guard. Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: For the most part, did you get along with the guards?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Some of the guards were good, yeah. But we had a... we had a Sergeant, and boy, that we used to call "Squeaky" and he... he was a miserable guy. We always screwed him up. When we... when we went outside. He used to, in the winter time... he was... when it was nice weather. He'd take a headcount in the barracks, but well, we couldn't do that. But sometimes when we went outside, some guys... he count us and then he'd recount us. Then he'd wonder why we got more men in the camp then we should. But he was the most miserable. I heard he got killed. See a couple of outfits -- guys that where in the... 90 of them... when they broke us in ten... ten... ten groups. They send... they got killed by the American fighter planes. They strafed them and they killed them. But we were lucky, they only hit us twice. That we... we heard the planes in a distance and we... we got in... off the road. Then when we were going from Stalag XII-A to II-B they... we were in Berlin, they put us in a marshalling yard, and they were bombing the marshalling yards, and bombs hit the ground and lift up... the box cars would lift up and come back on the track. It was lucky it come back on the track. But after the bombing they... they locked us in. Then -- then when the bombing was over they wanted us up to clean up... to clean up the area, and we'd just go like this, "we don't have to," and they didn't force us. They said, "okay." But a lot of times to get extra food we used to volunteer to do stuff. My buddy and I volunteered to... they had horses coming from the Russian front and they were wild. And my buddy got kicked in the chin. And they were... they were putting shoes on them, horseshoes, and anyway we were supposed to be holding them and the horse kicked him in the chin. And then we went back for lunch and come back. We were supposed to go back, and they were looking for us. We went in a couple of barracks. They couldn't find us. And then when... after they come back that night they went... they went... the Sergeant said, "where were you?" And we said, "oh, we forgot. We went to visit so and so and we forgot we were supposed to go."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What were the regular food ration like in the prison camps?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Well, it varied -- varied. Sometimes we got... when we were first in XII-A, we used to get soup made out of sugar beets and it was so sweet it was sickening. You couldn't even eat it. So we -- after that we never ate it. They made it out of sugar beet pulp. Then -- oh yeah, I was going to tell you, while we were there they had Indians from India. They were working in the mess hall. Anyway, we got a bad case... I'd say '80 percent of the guys in the camp got dysentery. We had a diarrhea... bad diarrhea. Well, our... they had a... they had a... two compounds there, latrines, they couldn't handle all of us. So the Germans let us go in where the indians were. And anyway, we were on the... sitting on the pot, and there were no toilets, they didn't have no toilet seat, just a toilet, you know, and plumbing. Anyway, these Indians, they would come in there, drop their pants, take a dump, then they would take... on the... right next to the toilet they had a bucket there. They used to wash their hands and then they go back into the kitchen and work. Well, we got... we got dysentery. I... I had that... I had that... well, the doctor called it... it was a... what the hell they call it? It was in my intestines... my colon.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: My colon was all scarred up from that because I had blood coming out of me.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right. Right.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Anyway, I tried to talk -- tell the VA, but they never did anything about that. Anyway so, after we left the camp and we... I still had that diarrhea. I'd sometimes... I had it. I... I went to the toilet. Even when we were on the road I had to run. See, they walked us for 40 minutes and then they give us 40 or 50 minutes and then they'd stop and give us a rest. And anyway they... we used to run in the fields and drop our pants and do our business. And then... and the German civilians were right in back of us. And those women, they didn't have no shame. They'd come out and drop their... drop their pants and they'd face us and doing their business. It didn't bother them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And then they -- all of a sudden they... they broke them off and we were by ourselves then. That was about four or five days while we were on the road. And then on top of that... and then whenever they found a dead horse, then we had meat for supper. They'd made soup out of the dead horse. Which, there was nothing wrong, the horse was just starved, you know, it was weak and...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did it taste like?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: You never ate horse meat?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Not that I know of. I might have.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: I'd tell you when we were in, I forget, it was Texas, every once in a while we'd get horse meat.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: It's real pink red.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. Yeah, I heard that.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And we used to get in Texas, horse meat. And then when on the road, it was real pink. The meat, it was real pink.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. Does it taste pretty much like beef?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Like beef, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: But they say that a cow, he'll drink anything. A horse is particular. Did you know that?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Could be better for you, I suppose.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: That -- that... it's a... it's a funny thing. Then in Camp Atterbury we used to get goat's meat.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Boy, that thing. When they frying like... it stunk like hell. It's... life is funny then.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah. Anything else?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Well, yeah when I -- when I had... when I was home on a furlough, I had a good... pretty good time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum. What did you do when you were back in Cleveland?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What did you do?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Well, I did a lot of running around and drinking. One... one night I ended up... we were in a bar over here on Broadway and 131st, and they closed the bar down at 3 o'clock... 3:30. We ended up in... in Erie, Pennsylvania.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Looking for a bar that was open?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: No, no, no, my -- one of the guys that we were with, he said, "let's take a ride." With my... I had a '37 Ford. Five of us, we ended up in... in Erie, Pennsylvania. We pulled up by the wharf there, was sleeping, and all of a sudden the guy's rapping on... it was... already it was about 9 o'clock. We were sleeping, and the guy pounding on the window, the policeman. He said, you're... you're breaking the law. Get out of here." Well, see we were all... we were all GIs. So there were three... three Army, one Marine, one sailor.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So that would have been what, about a two hour trip maybe?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yeah, old -- old 20. Route 20.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Route 20, no freeways then, exactly. You went right by my street on Route 20.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Where do you live?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I live in Meder (ph), right off Route 20.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Oh yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah, exactly.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yeah, like I said there -- on -- when Pearl Harbor... that I worked on a show.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: I started in 1938, and I left there -- well, I left there two weeks before I went in the Army. I worked... I was working two jobs in the factory and in the... in the show, I... either doorman or usher. Then I come out of the Army. I worked for a while. But I never paid to go in the shows. That's how I met my wife.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh really.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: In a show. That was in August of '45.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You think we got most of it? Oh, you know, yeah. Speaking of August '45, do you remember any big celebrations for VJ Day, when the war finally ended?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yeah, didn't I tell you?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Let's hear it.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: We -- I was... there was... Maple Heights, there was a roller rink... there used to be a roller rink on McCracken... McCracken and Thomas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Well, I used to -- when I was home on a furlough, I used to go there because I got to... got to... I loved to roller skate, and I got to know the manager. Well, he... I... he told... I... he had the same size shoes, you know, for to... roller skates, I had for the same foot... size. Anyway, he used to let me have roller skates. I roller skate. I never... he never charged me. So on VJ night I went there. And there was... there was about 10 of us. And we told the manager... manager... I said... and I told him, hey, not 'till my people come here. He said... so one guy suggested let's go to Liter drugstore in Bedford, and we bought four bottles of champagne, we all chipped in. And we... we brought them to the roller rink. We were drinking. All of a sudden this Bob Serney (ph), he said, "I got an idea." We were all... all of us were feeling good, you know. He said, "let's go downtown." So we all got in... in... there was... there was only one, two, three, four... there was two women and then three men. And I was the odd ball. Anyway, so we were in... went downtown. And you know where the... the... by the square, that monument is?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: We were sitting on top. We were all feeling good. Then we got off and we were standing right there by the... by the soldier's... the other monument. And all of a sudden you see a guy with a bottle and hand it to us. Because there was three... two of us were service... three of us were servicemen and the other guy... the guy that was the manager of the theater... he... he was a... he had something wrong with his... anyway, he was... anyway, he was 4Fing it. Anyway, but it... the women, they see you, boy, grabbed you, kiss you. And boy, I'd never forgot that day. We... I got home 6 o'clock in the morning. My... my dad was ready... he was getting ready to go to work. My brother-in-law, they were going to go to work. But it... it was a good union. Then well, like I said, VJ night we were in England, you know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: VE, right?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: VE, no, in Germany, but we --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: But England -- when I hit London, they still had blackout. But I... I had a Class A pass. I ended up one time... I didn't get back until 7 o'clock the next morning, and I got stopped by the MPs. I... I went with a woman. And she lived outside of London. And I met her about 8 o'clock that night, and I got back like... it was 7 o'clock and the MPs asked me, "where's your pass?" I pulled out my pass. He looked on Class

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Okay go, ahead. And on top they had PO... EX-POW on there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: But when I was interviewed in the hospital by CIA -- not CI

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And they fingerprinted me, see if I was really the person that they -- they... that I claimed to be.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And then when I -- then when I was in London, I got... they... I had to go again.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was that because of your name?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: No, no, no, because, see they -- they wanted to know could I be... I could have been a German...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: -- with the name and that. And anyway, see, the other one... the last guy... when the MPs pulled me over, they took me to the CI... CIC, and they fingerprinted me. And then they had my records right there, you know, in London. They said "you're... you're the one... you're not wanted." And then...

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you were on -- you were probably on the road when FDR died. Did you get the news right away?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yeah, yeah, the same day.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How did you get that news?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: The German, I -- they gave us a two day rest... three day rest.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And we were in an area they were -- it was going to be... they were building a building for the Nazis.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And my buddy and I volunteered to do carpenter work so, that we would get extra allowance of food.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Because we were always looking for some. Anyway, so my buddy and I would cut the piece of wood too short and odd pieces. And the German, the guy in charge, he said, "don't cut." He fired us. But he was a nice guy. He... I had bad a... I had bronchitis. I was coughing and coughing. And he said, "you see that tree there?" And I said, "yeah." He said, "go with them and get yourself..." it was a pine tree. You know that sap that leaks out?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: And he said, "chew it, take that and chew it." And he said, "you'll get rid of your cough." I did. You know what it is? Kerosene. That's how they make kerosene. Used to make kerosene out of a... out of a pine pitch.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: I don't know if you knew.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No. But it coats your throat or something?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Well, lot of people -- some of the old timers used to have you gargle with kerosene.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: But I -- I swallowed that thing. But life is funny. And we got married June 28th, 1947.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Um-hum.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: Two years after I come home. And I met my wife in the show, in old Maple Heights Theater. And well, she sat next... she was there with her sister and I was there with a sailor. And he come back from overseas, from Japan on a furlough. Anyway... anyway... no, he was in the European Theater. They didn't send him. Anyway, he sat... he was from Maple Heights. I knew him from a kid. Anyway, we were sitting there, my wife sat right next to me. And then we got to talk, and I said, "were you from?" And she said, "McCracken." I said, "where?" She said, "Nearly (ph) Road." And I thought "hey, you're lying. I was raised... born and raised there." But I forgot they built their house in '42. And then I remembered. And then I started apologizing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were gone.

sp.speaker: Edward F. Brandtner
sp.p: No, I told her I apologize. And she still said that I called her a liar. Then... then right after VJ night we went out a couple of times. And then I had to go. No, it was more than a couple of times. We dated for a while and then I went back to camp. And when we come back, I started dating. We steadying, steadying, steadying and then in '46 I gave her the engagement ring in October. Then we got married in June 28th, '47. I was 27-years-old.
